title: Senior's toolkit: the dotnet CLI and the debugger
summary: The commands and keys you use every day to create, run, build and step through a C# program.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: the dotnet CLI and the debugger
steps.body: At work you create, run and debug programs from the terminal and the IDE dozens of times a day. These are the commands and keys experienced C# developers reach for without thinking.

toolkit.what: Create a new project from a template. `dotnet new list` shows every template installed (console, classlib, xunit, webapi...).
flags: the project name, also used as the root namespace
the folder to create it in
the target framework; the default is the newest your SDK knows
toolkit.when: starting any new app, tool or experiment

toolkit.what: Build if needed, then run. Everything after a bare `--` goes to your program's `args`, not to `dotnet`.
flags: which project to run when you are not in its folder
stop reading dotnet options; the rest goes to your program
run the optimised build (the default is Debug)

toolkit.what: Run the app and rebuild it every time you save. Small edits are applied with hot reload, without a restart.
flags: always restart instead of patching the running app
(while it runs) force a full restart
toolkit.when: tweaking output or logic and wanting to see each change at once

toolkit.what: Compile and report every error and warning as `File.cs(line,col): error CSxxxx: message`. It is what CI runs first.
flags: fail on any warning, the way strict CI does
detailed log when a build fails for a reason you cannot see

toolkit.what: Add a NuGet package reference to the project file. .NET 10 also accepts the newer spelling `dotnet package add`.
flags: pin an exact version instead of the latest stable

toolkit.what: Project settings in the `.csproj` file. New projects already turn on nullable checks and implicit usings; strict teams also turn warnings into errors.
flags: warn (CS8602 and friends) when a value might be null
a warning fails the build, so nobody can ignore one
the common `using` lines are added for you

toolkit.what: The debugger keys in Visual Studio and VS Code. Stop on a line and look at every variable instead of guessing with `Console.WriteLine`.
flags: toggle a breakpoint on the current line
start debugging, or continue to the next breakpoint
step over a call / step into it
step out of the current method
toolkit.example: F9 on the line, F5 to run, hover a variable to see its value
toolkit.when: a value is wrong and you do not know where it goes wrong

steps.prompt: Match each option to what it does.
pairs: names the project and its namespace
picks the folder to create it in
runs a project from another folder
passes the rest of the line to your program

steps.prompt: Your program reads `args` and expects `--currency GBP`. You are at the repository root and the project is in `src/Till`. Complete the command.
steps.explain: `dotnet run` builds and runs. The bare `--` tells `dotnet` to stop reading options, so `--currency GBP` arrives in your program's `args`.

steps.prompt: The build prints this. What is wrong, and where?
code: src/Till/Program.cs(14,19): error CS0103: The name 'totl' does not exist in the current context
options: Line 14, column 19 of Program.cs uses `totl`, which is not declared: probably a typo for `total`
A package called `totl` is missing: run `dotnet add package totl`
The project file has an error in its 14th property
steps.explain: Compiler messages are `file(line,column): error CODE: message`. Read the first error first: later ones are often caused by it. CS0103 means the name is not in scope, which is usually a typo or a variable declared inside a block you have left.

steps.prompt: Your change builds fine on your laptop, but CI fails with `error CS8602: Dereference of a possibly null reference.` What is going on?
options: CI treats warnings as errors (`-warnaserror` or `TreatWarningsAsErrors`); locally CS8602 was only a warning you scrolled past
CI uses an older C# compiler that does not know about null
The CI machine has a different Nullable setting in its registry
steps.explain: The same code gives the same diagnostics everywhere; only the severity differs. Run `dotnet build -warnaserror` locally to reproduce CI, then fix the possible null (check it, or use `?.` / `??`) instead of silencing it.

steps.prompt: Which tool do you reach for first?
items: See each change to the receipt layout as soon as you save
Keep a console app re-running while you tune its output
Find out why `total` is 0 on the third pass of a loop
See the value of `price` just before the exception
Reproduce locally the build failure CI reported
Check there are no warnings before you push

steps.prompt: Put the steps of starting a small tool with one package in order. You start at the repository root.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Keep `dotnet watch` running while you shape code, and press F9 instead of adding a `Console.WriteLine` when a value surprises you. Before every push, run the same `dotnet build -warnaserror` that CI runs, so the failure happens on your machine, not in review.
